title: Security Analysis of Blocked Network Clients
text:
This paper analyzes security risk differences between wireless and wired network clients by examining blocked access attempts within a large university network environment. Clients attempting to access sites flagged as risky or inappropriate by institutional security controls are classified as higher-risk, providing a measurable proxy for security exposure.
Wireless clients are defined as devices connected via institutional Wi-Fi (guest or secure), while wired clients include devices connected through Ethernet infrastructure such as labs, libraries, and campus workstations. The central research question asks:

Given that a network client is denied access, which client type is denied access more frequently on average?

Using network security logs collected via Elasticsearch, the analysis demonstrates that wireless clients exhibit a higher average rate of denied access events, suggesting a higher relative risk classification compared to wired clients.

title: Security Analysis of Blocked Network Clients
text:
Methods Summary
Network security data was collected by developing a custom Python-based API that queried Elasticsearch clusters used by university security and network engineering teams. Due to the scale of the data (terabytes of log records), queries were constrained to three-day windows to avoid timeouts.
Key fields extracted include: - IP address, categorized by wireless or wired client ranges - Blocked event count, representing denied access attempts
The API returned aggregated JSON responses containing IP-level counts, which were then analyzed statistically to compare denial frequencies across client types.

title: Security Analysis of Blocked Network Clients
text:
Key Finding

Wireless network clients were denied access more frequently on average than wired clients, indicating higher exposure to blocked or risky destinations.

text:

I am, at my core, a builder. I love to create things that make a tangible, positive impact—whether that’s laying tile and framing walls in the physical world, or designing intelligent systems that orchestrate vast amounts of data in the digital one. My “why” is simple but powerful: to unite the physical and digital worlds into systems that think, sense, and act intelligently. I see engineering not just as solving problems, but as designing the “brain” of complex machines, organizations, and infrastructures.




My journey began in construction. From childhood through my undergrad years, I worked on remodeling homes and heavy civil projects—learning how things fit together, how systems interact, and how effort turns into something you can stand on. One day, while installing moisture sensors for an irrigation system, I had a spark of realization: data and computation could be as powerful a building material as wood, steel, and concrete. That insight set me on a new trajectory.
I went on to earn a degree in Applied Statistics and Computer Science at BYU, then launched into my career as a software engineer. The mindset I developed in construction—practical, hands-on, iterative—carried over into my technical career. I still think like a builder; I just build with code, data, and systems as much as with tools and materials.




My first professional chapter was in aerospace, working on satellite software for the Department of Defense. I focused on space situational awareness, developing image processing systems and leveraging optimization models (including vehicle routing problems for satellite scheduling). It gave me a front-row seat to the complexity of large-scale, mission-critical systems.
Later, I transitioned into cybersecurity, where I applied big-data analytics (at petabyte scale) and machine learning to track down malicious actors across massive networks. This work deepened my passion for intelligent systems—systems that don’t just monitor, but understand, detect, and adapt.
Today, I’m a systems engineer specializing in data architecture and engineering. I design and build data warehouses for business intelligence, architect pipelines for analytics, and lay the foundation for full data science ecosystems. My role blends engineering precision with systems-level thinking, bridging the gap between raw data and actionable intelligence.




I consider myself a systems-minded engineer, fluent in software engineering, intelligent systems, and cyber-physical integration (IoT, automation, AI/ML). My strongest technical roots are in Linux and Python (with 10 years of professional experience), but I’m deliberately language- and tool-agnostic. For me, technology is a toolkit—I learn what’s needed to build what I envision.
Some highlights of what I’ve built include:

A full-stack network monitoring application for network engineers and cybersecurity teams.
A data catalog platform from scratch, including the data crawler backend and search-enabled frontend.
Prototyped ML models for detecting malicious cyber activities at scale.
An Android application using blockchain technologies to support humanitarian assistance.
IoT-to-mobile applications connecting physical sensors with cloud and mobile platforms.
CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure-as-code deployments for complex workloads.
Containerized and Kubernetes-based systems to operationalize image processing and analytics within a cloud native environment.
Data visualization prototypes and mockups for executive and engineering audiences.
Leadership roles guiding software teams through development, deployment, and production.
Two entire homes from the ground up.
Too many to count construction projects. On the side and as I have time I might do one every month or so.

At heart, I’m a project-based learner and builder. I’ve been fortunate to work across satellites, cybersecurity, data platforms, and intelligent infrastructure, and every project has sharpened my ability to think across domains.




My dream is to revolutionize the construction industry and take it into an Industry 4.0/5.0 era, leveraging every available technology—from robotics and IoT to AI and digital twins. I want to bridge the gap between robots that can move and systems that can think. Others build machines and algorithms; I want to design the optimization, orchestration, and simulation frameworks that make them work together at scale.
Using operations research, decision intelligence, digital twins, and systems AI, I aim to turn isolated automation into orchestrated, intelligent workflows—optimizing site logistics, safety, and long‑term cost efficiency. My mission is to pioneer systems‑scale intelligence that unites humans, machines, and AI into adaptive, resilient infrastructures—first across construction tech, and then extending to aerospace, industrial operations, and beyond.




I see this as a mission bigger than myself, and one that requires collaboration. If my story resonates with you—whether you’re an engineer, researcher, entrepreneur, or builder in any domain—I invite you to connect with me. Let’s build together, share ideas, and push the boundaries of what’s possible in intelligent, cyber-physical systems.

title: Gurobipy Transportation LP Solver
text:
Project Overview
This project demonstrates how to formulate and solve a transportation Linear Programming (LP) problem using the Gurobi optimization solver with its Python API (gurobipy). It was created as a learning exercise in optimization modeling, exploring LP formulation, constraint setup, and solution retrieval for classic network flow problems such as minimum-cost transportation.
The repository includes: - Python code implementing the transportation LP model. - Utility and helper modules for data handling. - A written report discussing modeling decisions and results.
The transportation problem classically seeks to minimize total shipping cost while satisfying supply and demand constraints across origins and destinations — a staple use case for LP solvers in operations research.

title: Gurobipy Transportation LP Solver
text:
What You’ll Find Inside

Problem formulation: Setting up decision variables, objective functions, and linear constraints representing supply, demand, and flow balance.
Gurobi integration: Leveraging the gurobipy API to build and solve the optimization model.
Reports & practice code: Supporting analysis of solver outputs and insights gained while learning LP concepts.

title: Identifying High-Demand Utilities in Virginia: Statistical Learning and National Comparative Analysis in the Era of Data Centers
text: Power & Data Centers

title: Identifying High-Demand Utilities in Virginia: Statistical Learning and National Comparative Analysis in the Era of Data Centers
text:
Paper Overview
This study examines how the rapid expansion of data centers is reshaping electricity demand in Virginia relative to national utility trends. Using ten years of U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA-861) data, the project applies statistical learning and machine-learning methods to identify high-demand electric utilities and characterize emerging load patterns associated with commercial and industrial growth.
Key techniques include engineered intensity metrics, supervised classification models (logistic regression, ridge regression, random forests, KNN), and unsupervised methods (PCA and K-means). Results indicate that Virginia exhibits a higher concentration of load-intensive utilities once demand is weighted by commercial activity—consistent with observed data center expansion—while ridge-regularized and tree-based models provide the most stable and interpretable performance.

title: Characterizing Volumetric DDoS Attacks in IoT Traffic
text:
Project Overview
This project investigates volumetric Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attack patterns in Internet of Things (IoT) network traffic using the publicly available IoT23 dataset. The analysis characterizes how attack traffic behaves at scale, identifies key traffic features indicative of volumetric flooding, and demonstrates methods for profiling and distinguishing DDoS attack flows from normal IoT communications.
The repository includes: - A detailed written report summarizing the study and findings (PDF). - Data processing and analysis code in Python and R. - Traffic diagrams and supporting artifacts illustrating attack characterization. - Supporting scripts for data ingestion and transformation.
